I’m a 42-year-old man who has farmed these plots in Quzhou since I left school. Like most households around here, I hold about ten mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, so the only sensible thing is the winter wheat–summer maize rotation everyone has done for generations. You don’t gamble with cotton or vegetables unless you have tunnels and buyers lined up, and I don’t. 

For wheat, I’ll sow **Luyuan 502**, an improved variety that performs steadily in our dry springs. I’ll rotary-till the field in late September and put down basal compound fertilizer (about 50 kg of 15-15-15 per mu) before sowing around October 5–10. After the turn of the year I’ll top-dress with urea at green-up and again at jointing, which brings total nitrogen to roughly 28 kg N per mu, phosphorus to about 12 kg P₂O₅ per mu, and potassium to about 10 kg K₂O per mu. Wheat needs water at critical moments, so I’ll irrigate four times: once right after sowing if the soil is dry, once before winter dormancy, once at jointing in March, and once at grain filling in May. I expect about 1,050 kg per mu if the spring drought doesn’t bite too hard. For weeds and pests, I’ll spray a herbicide once after sowing, insecticide twice (aphids and armyworm), and a fungicide once at heading—four applications in total.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I’ll no-till drill **Denghai 605** hybrid maize straight into the stubble. Time is short between crops, and no-tillage saves diesel and keeps moisture. I’ll apply another 50 kg per mu of compound fertilizer at sowing and top-dress with urea at the big-flare stage, giving the maize about 24 kg N, 10 kg P₂O₅, and 8 kg K₂O per mu. Maize drinks less than wheat here, so two irrigations—one at jointing and one at silking—are usually enough. I’ll spray herbicide once, insecticide twice (mainly corn borer), so three pesticide rounds altogether. With decent August rains, I should get about 1,100 kg per mu.

That is my plan. It is safe, proven, and fits the ten mu I have.
